citation: Raffoul, F. (2019). The Ethics of Moods. In C. Hadjioannou (Ed.), Heidegger on Affect (Philosophers in Depth, pp. 245–264). Palgrave Macmillan. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-24639-6_11
thesis: Argues that Heidegger's ontology of moods (Stimmungen/Befindlichkeit) harbors an implicit ethics: to find oneself in a mood is already to be called to an original responsibility. Confronts and resolves the paradox that moods' radical opacity, withdrawal, and expropriation seem to foreclose any ethical appropriation, by showing that this very inappropriability is what opens responsibility -- Dasein must take over ('carry') a facticity, thrownness, and finitude it did not choose and cannot master. Concludes that 'the ethics of moods' names a responsibility for finitude itself, contrasted explicitly with the Kantian model of a self-originating responsible subject. Chapter authored by François Raffoul; Hadjioannou is the volume editor only. Never mentions boredom (Langeweile) or Heidegger's FCM three-form boredom analysis by name; illustrates its general theory of mood via homesickness, joy, hope, and elevated/depressed moods instead.

sections.title: Ontological status of moods restated (never psychological/inner); moods determine thinking itself (homesickness as fundamental mood of philosophizing, 1929/30 course); states the 'ethics of moods' thesis and its central paradox (opacity vs. responsibility)

Ontological character of disposition (Befindlichkeit) per BT §29: primordial self-disclosure prior to cognition/volition/reflection; critique of moods as a subordinate 'third class' of experience; rejection of moods as subjective coloring of an objective world and of the term 'affect' itself; moods as neither inside nor outside, constitutive of Dasein's being

Sharpened paradox: moods beyond will/cognition, 'one does not know why'; the motif of mood as burden (Last), from the 1921-22 Aristotle courses' 'difficulty of factical life' through BT's elevated/depressed moods; Agamben's facticius/nativus etymology of facticity as non-originarity; birth and thrownness (BT §72) as Heidegger's ontological name for natality

The hinge: Derrida on responsibility arising from aporia; Heidegger's marginal note to SZ 134 glossing 'burden' as the charge of Dasein's responsibility; thrownness (Geworfenheit) as what is felt in a mood (via Sheehan); withdrawal itself as an event that calls Dasein; being-guilty (Schuldigsein, BT §58) as taking over an unmasterable thrownness -- the paradox of being a 'thrown basis'

Moods disclose Dasein's finitude as groundlessness (Grundlosigkeit); explicit contrast with the Kantian self-originating-subject model of responsibility; final formulation: ethics of moods as responsibility for finitude itself, assuming rather than overcoming moods' mystery

Four endnotes (translation note; Befindlichkeit terminology; 1929/30 course block-quote on the psychologizing of feeling; Derrida citation) and a short reference list: Agamben (2002), Derrida (2008), Sheehan (2018)

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: analogical only (P/anticipatory-application) -- boredom is never mentioned; Raffoul's extended 'burden'/'difficulty of factical life' motif (GA 61:100-108, drawing on the 1921-22 Aristotle-interpretation courses) describes an existential weight structurally akin to meaninglessness-as-boredom's-core, but the chapter itself never names boredom

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: analogical only (P/anticipatory-application) -- the remark that elevated moods are possible only in an 'ecstatic-temporal relation... to the thrown ground' (SZ 345) gestures at mood's temporal structure in general, not boredom's time-drag specifically

constructs.label: profound/deep boredom (FCM 3rd form)
constructs.treatment: chapter-level textual-contiguity bridge only (P/anticipatory-application), not a content engagement -- see bridges.fcm and the 'Reading of FCM' discussion in the .md; Raffoul draws his general Grundstimmung theory from the same GA 29/30 course whose later Part One develops the three-form boredom analysis, but he never discusses boredom itself

constructs.label: boredom proneness
constructs.treatment: not treated by the chapter; used only as the target construct of a Part III methodological caveat this unit draws from Raffoul's critique of the term 'affect' (P/anticipatory-application)

readings.text: Moods are not psychological add-ons but disclose an ontological truth of Dasein; 'Dasein is always already in a mood' and existence is never neutral, always already 'moved' by a mood.

Moods determine thinking itself: philosophical concepts must be extracted anew each time out of a basic disposition (Grundstimmung); without it, conceptual work collapses into 'a forced clatter of concepts.'

The 1929/30 course names homesickness (das Heimweh) as the fundamental mood of philosophizing; philosophizing is comprehensive questioning arising out of Dasein's being 'gripped,' possible only from within a Grundstimmung.

Raffoul's thesis: to be thrown in a mood already engages a response, an original responsibility -- an 'ethics of moods' -- which must confront the objection that moods' opacity forecloses any ethical appropriation.
Disposition (Befindlichkeit) is the ontological characterization of the ontical phenomenon 'mood'; it discloses Dasein to itself prior to, and beyond the range of, all cognition and volition.
Disposition is not arrived at by reflection turning back on itself; rather it is what first makes any subsequent reflection on inner 'experiences' (Erlebnisse) possible at all.

Every comportment is always already in some attunement beforehand; attunement (Gestimmtheit) simply is relationality (Bezogensein) -- each new attunement only a re-attunement of one already unfolding.

Rejects the traditional schema ranking feeling as a subordinate 'third class' of experience beneath thinking and willing, and the picture of moods as subjective coloring added onto an already-constituted objective world.

Heidegger rejects the very term 'affect' (Affizierung, an external impression made upon someone): joy, for instance, is not brought upon Dasein from outside but belongs to its own ecstatic relationship to world.
Moods are neither 'inside' nor 'outside': a mood 'assails' Dasein and arises out of being-in-the-world; far from an inconstant accompaniment, mood gives Dasein subsistence in its very foundations.

Moods lead Dasein before the pure 'that' of its There, which 'stares at it with the inexorability of an enigma'; one cannot know why one is in a given mood because the whence and whither remain obscure.
Only a counter-mood can master a mood (an insight credited to Spinoza), and even such mastery never frees Dasein of mood as such.

Mood is a burden (Last): being becomes manifest as a burden even in elevated/alleviating moods, which presuppose rather than escape it -- e.g. hope brings relief yet remains related to a burden in the mode of having-been.

The burden of mood traces back to the 1921-22 Aristotle-interpretation courses' account of factical life as constitutively 'hard to bear,' whose tendency to make itself easy for itself is a flight from, not a refutation of, this weight.

Via Agamben's etymology, facticity (facticius: made, produced, hence non-original) is opposed to nativus (natural, given by birth); Dasein can never appropriate the being it is, a being to which it remains irreparably consigned.

Thrownness is Heidegger's ontological name for birth/natality (BT §72's 'Being-towards-the-beginning'); Dasein exists as born yet cannot get behind its own thrownness to release its 'that-it-is-and-has-to-be' from itself.

Derrida's claim, endorsed by Raffoul: ethical responsibility arises constitutively from aporia and paradox, not despite it -- the project of an 'ethics of moods' should therefore not be abandoned merely because it appears aporetic.
Even what is not under Dasein's own decision must in some way be 'retrievingly appropriated,' even if only by putting up with or shirking it.

The pivotal textual anchor: Heidegger's marginal note to SZ 134 glosses 'burden' (Last) as das Zu-tragende ('what has to be carried') and states the human being is charged with the responsibility of Dasein, appropriated by it; to carry is to take over one's belonging to being itself.
Thrownness (Geworfenheit) names what is felt, precisely, in a mood -- per Sheehan, thrownness 'bespeaks' Befindlichkeit, the a priori fact that we are affectively attuned.

Withdrawal is not mere absence but an event in its own right, which may concern and claim Dasein more essentially than anything present; it is this event of withdrawal, not positive presence, that calls Dasein to responsibility.

Agamben distinguishes Heidegger's Faktizitat sharply from Husserl's Tatsachlichkeit (mere contingent factuality of intraworldly objects): for Heidegger the proper trait of facticity is not Zufalligkeit but Verfallenheit, and Dasein, unlike Sartre's subject, must itself be its 'there.'

Culminates in Schuldigsein (being-guilty): Dasein has been brought into its 'there' but not of its own accord, and can never get its own basis into its power -- yet as existing it must take over being-a-basis. This is the paradox of being a 'thrown basis.'
Moods disclose Dasein's finitude as groundlessness (Grund-losigkeit) and concealment of the ground (Grund-verborgenheit).

Explicit contrast with Kant: responsibility is not grounded in being the absolute origin of a causal series to whom actions are ascribed, but in being thrown into an existence one does not originate yet must answer for.

Final formulation: the ethics of moods is a responsibility for finitude itself -- a being-responsible that consists not in overcoming moods but in assuming their mystery and respecting their secret, being their enigma.

concepts.gloss: mood / fundamental (grounding) mood; the fundamental way Dasein is as Dasein, never merely psychological
the ontological characterization of the ontical phenomenon 'mood'; primordial self-disclosure prior to cognition and volition
the character of Dasein's being -- its 'that it is' -- veiled in whence/whither yet disclosed in itself; what is felt in a mood; Heidegger's ontological name for birth/natality
the weight of facticity manifest in having a mood; das Zu-tragende, 'what has to be carried'; the site where the marginal note reintroduces responsibility
Dasein's facticity, marked by Verfallenheit, sharply distinguished (via Agamben) from the mere contingent factuality (Zufalligkeit) of objectively present, intraworldly things (Husserl's sense)
the taking-over of one's own unmasterable thrownness; the paradox of being a 'thrown basis' one must nonetheless take over as one's own
withdrawal understood not as mere absence but as an event that calls and claims Dasein, possibly more essentially than anything present
the chapter's own thesis-term: the claim that being-in-a-mood is itself the site of an original ethical responsibility for one's own facticity and finitude

interlocutors.name: Martin Heidegger
interlocutors.role: primary text under analysis across SZ (Being and Time), GA 29/30 (FCM), GA 65 (Beitrage/Contributions), GA 89 (Zollikon Seminars), GA 27 (Einleitung in die Philosophie), GA 61 (early Aristotle-interpretation courses), GA 39 (Holderlin's Hymns), GA 8 (What Is Called Thinking?), and GA 11 (What Is Philosophy?)

interlocutors.name: Giorgio Agamben
interlocutors.role: 'The Passion of Facticity' (2002) supplies the facticius/nativus etymology and the Husserl/Sartre-vs.-Heidegger contrast (Tatsachlichkeit/Zufalligkeit vs. Faktizitat/Verfallenheit) that grounds Raffoul's expropriation thesis

interlocutors.name: Jacques Derrida
interlocutors.role: The Gift of Death (2008): ethical responsibility arises constitutively from aporia and paradox -- the key move licensing Raffoul's claim that moods' very opacity opens (rather than forecloses) an ethics

interlocutors.name: Thomas Sheehan
interlocutors.role: 'But What Comes Before the After?' (2018), cited for the claim that thrownness 'bespeaks' Befindlichkeit as the a priori fact of affective attunement to world; a different Sheehan publication from his own Ch.2 chapter in this same volume

interlocutors.name: Immanuel Kant
interlocutors.role: contrast case in the Conclusion: the model of a responsible subject as the absolute self-originating cause of a series of actions, which Raffoul explicitly rejects in favor of thrown responsibility

interlocutors.name: Rene Descartes
interlocutors.role: contrast case: 'pure inspection of the mind alone' under 'clear and distinct ideas' as the intellectualist picture of thought Heidegger's mood-disposed thinking opposes

interlocutors.name: Baruch Spinoza
interlocutors.role: credited with the insight that only a counter-mood, never sheer will or cognition, can master a mood

tensions.label: Psychologism vs. ontology of mood
tensions.poles: the traditional view of moods/feelings as a fleeting, subjective 'third class' of experience beneath reason and will, merely coloring an already-objective world, vs. Heidegger's/Raffoul's view of mood as an ontologically primordial, world-disclosive structure prior to any subject-object split

tensions.label: Opacity vs. appropriability of moods
tensions.poles: moods' radical obscurity, unintelligibility, and withdrawal seem to foreclose any cognitive or practical appropriation and hence any ethical responsiveness, vs. Raffoul's resolution that this very expropriation is what opens and obligates an original responsibility

tensions.label: Self-causing subject vs. thrown responsibility
tensions.poles: the Kantian model, where responsibility presupposes being the absolute origin of a causal series of actions, vs. Raffoul's model, where responsibility arises from being thrown into an existence one does not originate yet must answer for
